source.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for Learning Assurance of a Vision-Based Landing System
source.authors: Romeo Valentin; O. Bruvik; Marc R. Schlichting; M. Kochenderfer

record.tranche_reason: The study assumes sparse directional representations and uses K-SVD dictionary atoms as a tool for interpretability and runtime monitoring; it does not test the superposition claims or their proposed alternatives.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a sparse dictionary fit to vision-transformer patch embeddings, but does not test whether the model naturally stores excess features as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, whether sparsity or importance changes that geometry, or whether the learned atoms are canonical features. The dictionary-fit reconstruction result is recorded under fits_no_version. Head-reliance and OOMS results concern the paper's assurance method, not the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study assumes the linear representation hypothesis and sparse superposed directions, and uses a K-SVD dictionary as a tool for content/style analysis and runtime monitoring. Its results concern its own assurance method (head-reliance split, OOMS AUROC), not whether superposition holds. It studies one vision transformer, not an LLM, so V4 as worded (LLMs) is not tested. The >90% reconstruction from 8 of 512 atoms is a dictionary-fit quality number, and no baseline (e.g. PCA or random dictionary) is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that K-SVD atoms split into contentful and stylistic types via cross-subset invariance. The regression head places about 82% of its reliance on contentful atoms (80% for the from-scratch model, statistically indistinguishable). An OOMS monitor using 34 of 512 atoms reaches AUROC 0.96, with 78% of selected atoms contentful. They make no claims about superposition mechanisms or canonical features.
record.recipe_differences: Uses K-SVD and Matching Pursuit on a vision-transformer representation for interpretability and runtime monitoring, rather than testing toy networks for superposition geometry, interference, or sparsity-dependent transitions.
record.method_sensitivity: The OOMS classifier's L1 regularization sweep changes the number of selected atoms and the contentful fraction; this is not a test of the claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: In a fine-tuned DINOv2-S, a 512-atom K-SVD dictionary with sparsity 8 explains over 90% of variance in the 384-d patch embeddings (importance-sampled held-out batch).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision-transformer patch embeddings can be well approximated by an overcomplete sparse dictionary (an indirect-evidence analogue of V4 for vision models).

record.problems: The study covers a single task and architecture. The authors note that the four dataset domains may not span stylistic variation, and that dictionary coverage and stability across retraining seeds remain future work. They also identify per-atom ablation or activation scrubbing as future work; the reported dictionary fit alone does not establish that its atoms are unique or canonical model features.

untested.parts: Toy-model geometry, sparsity-dependent phase transition, near-orthogonality and interference: none are measured.
Capacity or importance as the cause of polysemanticity is not examined.
No alternative mechanisms for polysemantic neurons are tested.
No LLM is studied. The ViT dictionary fit is recovered sparse structure only in a vision model, and is not tested against a baseline.
Atom completeness, stability across seeds and canonicity are not tested; the authors list these as future work.
No comparison of 1-D directions with multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The Toy Models of Superposition paper is cited only as background. Per-atom causal tests (ablation or activation scrubbing), a dictionary coverage analysis and seed stability are all deferred to future work, so nothing bears on V5.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, sparsity-dependent transitions, regular geometry, and interference are not tested.
The study does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
The study does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity indicates superposition.
The model studied is a vision transformer, not an LLM; the study does not test feature distribution across LLM neurons or SAE recovery in LLMs.
The study uses K-SVD rather than an SAE and does not test feature completeness, stability, or canonical status.
The study represents embeddings with dictionary atoms but does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: pretrained then fine-tuned model
rows.stage_stated: pretrained on LVD-142M, then fine-tuned end-to-end
rows.operation_detail: Fit a 512-atom K-SVD dictionary and sparse-code patch embeddings with a per-embedding sparsity of 8; evaluate reconstruction on a held-out batch.

conditions.value: held-out batch of the importance-sampled patch-embedding pool

rows.note: This quantifies how well the fitted sparse dictionary approximates the embeddings. Because the decomposition is learned by K-SVD, this result does not establish that the model natively represents semantic features in this geometry.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. This is a fit-quality number for the study's own K-SVD tool on a ViT, not an LLM, and has no baseline. It also covers only an importance-sampled pool (CLS plus top-4 patches per image), not all embeddings.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
